Chapter 3: The Internet’s Role in Self-Mythologizing and Performance
Let’s explore something that’s become almost second nature for so many of us—the way the internet invites all of us to step into the spotlight, whether we realize it or not.
It’s funny, isn’t it? The promise was always connection and information at our fingertips. But in reality, these platforms have turned us into performers, with audiences watching our every move. The louder you are, the more dramatic your story—the bigger the reward.
And somewhere along the way, the boundary between what’s true and what’s just for show can get a little blurry.
Picture this: you’re scrolling through your feed, taking in a parade of bright, polished snapshots and clever captions. Everyone seems confident, like they’ve got it all figured out. But here’s the thing—those images? They’re the result of a whole bunch of choices.
What to include, what to leave out, and how to frame every single moment so it looks just right. It’s no wonder there’s pressure to keep up. Sometimes, it means adding a little extra sparkle—or even making things up—just to stand out.
The internet really encourages us to become our own storytellers, turning even the most ordinary moments into something that’s meant to impress. The more you share, the more vulnerable or outrageous you are, the more attention you get.
And after a while, it’s tough to tell where real feelings end and performance begins. The craving for attention can push people to exaggerate their struggles, turning pain into content.
You can see this especially in online activism. There was a time when supporting a cause meant showing up in person, taking action in the real world. Now, you can join in with just a click or a share.
It’s so easy to signal your values, to show you’re on the “right” side—without ever leaving your couch. Morality becomes a performance too, traded for likes, shares, and new followers.
But here’s something to think about—the rewards for all this online performing? They don’t last long. Algorithms always want something new, and yesterday’s big moment fades fast. Trying to keep up can leave you feeling burned out, anxious, and even kind of empty.
The internet might promise connection, but a lot of times, it just feeds a sense of competition. It can feel like everyone else is living a better, fuller, more meaningful life.
For most of us, it’s almost impossible not to want to show off the perfect life online. After all, the tools make it so easy to crop out anything messy or unflattering. But if you’re always curating, always editing, it comes at a price.
The more you perform, the harder it is to remember what’s actually real. That mindset doesn’t stay online, either—it trickles into how you talk, how you think, even how you feel about yourself.
Most people don’t even notice just how much the internet has changed the way they see themselves. These platforms turn self-surveillance into a habit—constantly watching, judging, tweaking your own image.
Wanting to be seen, to get that approval, starts shaping choices and relationships in ways that can be tough to break free from.
